title: Daniel's Prayer and the Seventy Weeks
summary: Reading Jeremiah's prophecy that Jerusalem's desolation would last seventy years, Daniel turns to God in fasting and prays one of the Bible's great prayers of confession, pleading for the ruined city and sanctuary on the ground of God's mercy alone. While he is still praying, the angel Gabriel arrives with an answer: seventy weeks (usually understood as seventy sevens of years) are decreed for Jerusalem, ending in atonement and everlasting righteousness but passing through the cutting off of an anointed one and the destruction of the city.
story: Chapters 7 and 8 showed Daniel empires rising and a fierce ruler attacking God's sanctuary, and chapter 8 ended with Daniel sick and bewildered. Chapter 9 turns from vision to Scripture and prayer. Babylon has just fallen to the Medes and Persians, and Daniel, now an old man who was carried off as a youth, realizes that the seventy years Jeremiah foretold are nearly complete. The exile is ending, but Daniel does not simply wait for it. He confesses the sin that caused it, taking his place among the guilty. God's answer widens his view: the return from Babylon will not be the end of Israel's troubles. A longer period lies ahead before sin is finally dealt with, and the rest of the book (chapters 10 to 12) fills in what those years will hold.
historical:
The chapter is dated to the first year of Darius the Mede, the ruler the book places over Babylon after its fall in 539 BC (5:31). His identity is debated: some identify him with Gubaru, the governor Cyrus installed over Babylon, some with Cyrus himself under another title, and critical scholars regard him as a literary figure drawn from later Persian kings. The book's introduction discusses the question. The year is roughly 539 or 538 BC, the year Cyrus issued the decree that allowed exiles to return (Ezra 1:1-4).

Daniel's starting point is Jeremiah, who had prophesied that Judah would serve Babylon seventy years and that God would then bring his people home (Jeremiah 25:11-12; 29:10). Counted from the first deportation in about 605 BC, the seventy years come close to Cyrus's decree; counted from the temple's destruction in 587 or 586 BC, they reach roughly to its rebuilding, completed in 516 or 515 BC. Either way, the number was a round figure for a lifetime of exile, and Daniel reads it as a promise about to come due. The prophecy of seventy weeks that answers him is one of the most debated passages in the Bible. Its main readings are set out under the hard question below. Whatever their differences, all of them locate its climax in a real crisis for Jerusalem and its temple: the desecration under the Seleucid king Antiochus IV in 167 BC, the death of Jesus and the Roman destruction of the temple in AD 70, or a final crisis still to come.
cultural:
Daniel prays with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes, the standard signs of mourning and repentance in Israel and its neighbors: coarse cloth worn against the skin, ashes on the head, food refused. His prayer draws heavily on Deuteronomy and on Solomon's prayer at the dedication of the temple, which asked God to hear exiles who confessed their sin and prayed toward the land, the city, and the house built for his name (1 Kings 8:46-51). Daniel had kept that practice, praying toward Jerusalem three times a day (6:10). Gabriel arrives about the time of the evening sacrifice, although no sacrifice had been offered in Jerusalem for decades; the old rhythm of temple worship still shaped the prayer life of the exiles.

The prayer's logic is the covenant's logic. Moses had warned that disobedience would bring curses, including defeat and exile (Leviticus 26; Deuteronomy 28), and promised that confession would bring God's remembrance (Leviticus 26:40-45). When Daniel says that the curse written in the Law of Moses has been poured out, he is not complaining; he is agreeing with God's verdict. Prayers of this kind, communal confessions spoken by a leader on behalf of the people, also appear in Ezra 9, Nehemiah 1 and 9, and later Jewish prayer.
literary: The chapter has three parts: Daniel's reading of Scripture (verses 1-3), his prayer (verses 4-19), and Gabriel's answer (verses 20-27). The prayer itself is carefully built. It moves from God's greatness and covenant faithfulness to a long confession (the verbs pile up: sinned, done wrong, acted wickedly, rebelled, turned away), then to an admission that God is righteous in judging, and finally to urgent petition that rises to a climax in verse 19. Its refrain is contrast: to God belong righteousness and compassion; to us, shame. The prayer grounds every request in God's own character and name, not in Israel's merit: “we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion.” Gabriel's answer is poetry of a compressed, allusive kind, built on a play with sevens: Jeremiah's seventy years become seventy weeks, divided into seven, sixty-two, and one.

outline.t: Daniel reads Jeremiah and turns to prayer
Confession: God is righteous, and we have sinned
Petition: for your sake, restore your city
Gabriel comes while Daniel is still praying

doctrines.note: Daniel's prayer is shaped by Scripture, begins with God's character, confesses sin honestly, and appeals to God's mercy and reputation. Knowing that God had promised restoration did not make Daniel passive; it moved him to pray for what God had promised.

Daniel had lived faithfully, yet he confesses Israel's sin as his own: “we have sinned and done wrong.” Biblical repentance includes agreeing with God's judgment and taking responsibility for the sins of one's community, not only one's private failings.

Gabriel's six purposes for the seventy weeks (verse 24) include putting an end to sin and making atonement for iniquity. Return from exile will not solve the deeper problem that caused it; God himself must deal with sin.

Verses 25-26 speak of an anointed one, a prince, who will be cut off. Christians have long read this as a prophecy of Jesus, while others identify the figure with a priest or ruler of the Second Temple period; the options are set out below.

words.note: Shavua, a week, literally a unit of seven. Here it almost certainly means seven years, so that seventy weeks equals 490 years, an extension of Jeremiah's seventy by a factor of seven. The pattern echoes the sabbatical year and the Jubilee (Leviticus 25), and the exile itself was linked to the land's unkept sabbaths (2 Chronicles 36:21). Whether the numbers are exact chronology or symbolic periods is the central question of the chapter.

Mashiach, anointed one, the word behind Messiah. In the Old Testament it names priests, kings, and once the Persian Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1). In verses 25-26 the Hebrew has no article, so it can be read as an anointed one, a leader, rather than the title the Messiah. Translations that capitalize it, as the BSB does, reflect the Christian reading.

Hesed, covenant faithfulness, which the BSB renders loving devotion. Daniel's prayer opens by confessing that God keeps his covenant of loving devotion. The whole appeal rests on it: Israel has broken the covenant, but God's steadfast loyalty is the ground on which Daniel dares to ask.

Shiqquts, an abomination, a word used for idols and detestable objects of pagan worship. The abomination that causes desolation (verse 27; also 11:31 and 12:11) became a byword for the desecration of God's sanctuary. Jesus used it for the coming destruction of the temple (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14).

christ: Christians from the early centuries onward have read verses 24-27 as pointing to Jesus: an anointed one who comes after sixty-nine weeks, is cut off and has nothing, and after whom the city and sanctuary are destroyed, as happened in AD 70. On that reading the purposes of verse 24 (to put an end to sin, make atonement, bring in everlasting righteousness) are what Christ accomplished by his death and resurrection. Not all interpreters agree that the passage predicts Jesus specifically, and the arithmetic is disputed. But even on other readings the chapter's direction is clear: Israel's deepest need is not return from exile but atonement, and that need is met by God's mercy, not human merit, which is the pattern the New Testament sees completed in Christ. Jesus himself took up the chapter's phrase the abomination that causes desolation when he warned of Jerusalem's coming fall (Matthew 24:15).

hard.q: What are the seventy weeks, and who is the anointed one who is cut off?
hard.a:
The historical-critical reading, held by most modern scholars, reads the weeks against the second century BC. The seven weeks run from Jeremiah's word (around 587 BC) to an anointed leader after the exile, often Cyrus or the high priest Joshua. The anointed one cut off after sixty-two more weeks is the high priest Onias III, deposed and later murdered around 171 BC (2 Maccabees 4). The prince who is to come is Antiochus IV, whose half week of desecration began in 167 BC. Defenders grant that the numbers do not add up exactly and treat them as schematic.

The traditional messianic reading, held by many church fathers, most Reformers, and many interpreters today, counts sixty-nine weeks from a Persian decree to rebuild Jerusalem (often Artaxerxes' decree to Ezra, about 458 or 457 BC) to the ministry of Jesus in the early first century AD. The anointed one cut off is Christ crucified; the people of the prince who destroy the city are the Romans of AD 70; and the covenant confirmed for one week is often read as the new covenant, with sacrifice brought to an end by Christ's death.

The dispensational reading, influential among many evangelicals since the nineteenth century, agrees that the sixty-nine weeks end with the Messiah, often counted from Artaxerxes' decree to Nehemiah in about 445 BC using years of 360 days. It then sees a gap between the sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks, covering the present age. The seventieth week is still future: a coming ruler, the Antichrist, will make a seven-year covenant and break it halfway through.

Each reading has strengths and difficulties: the critical view fits the book's focus on Antiochus but must treat the numbers loosely; the messianic view explains verse 24's large purposes but must choose among starting dates; the dispensational view keeps the numbers literal but must posit an unmentioned gap. Faithful readers differ here, and the chapter's main point, that God will finally deal with sin, stands on each.

questions: Daniel read a promise in Scripture and responded by praying harder, not by waiting passively. How does knowing what God has promised shape the way you pray?
Daniel confesses sins he did not personally commit as though they were his own. What would it look like to pray that way for your family, church, or nation?
The prayer rests entirely on God's compassion and name, not on the people's righteousness. Why is that the only safe ground for asking anything of God?
